title: Reduce inhaled-steroid oral effects
stem: A client starts an inhaled corticosteroid and asks how to reduce mouth irritation and thrush risk. Which actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
options: Reserve every dose for episodes of wheezing
Brush the mouthpiece with a wet brush before each inhalation
Rinse the mouth and spit after each prescribed dose
Use a compatible spacer if prescribed for the device
Swallow the rinse water to improve lung absorption
why: A prescribed controller schedule is not the same as rescue use.
Cleaning must follow the device instructions; improvised wet cleaning may impair function.
Removing oral residue reduces local steroid exposure.
A spacer can reduce oropharyngeal deposition with suitable metered-dose inhalers.
Swallowed residue does not improve delivery to the lungs.
takeaway: Removing oral residue reduces local steroid exposure.
learningObjective: Teach local adverse-effect prevention while preserving prescribed controller treatment.

title: Clarify an asthma controller gap
stem: A client's asthma list contains a long-acting beta agonist alone. No inhaled corticosteroid or combination controller is documented. What is appropriate?
options: Teach the client to use it for every sudden attack
Confirm the regimen from the bronchodilator's colour
Plan follow-up based only on today's lack of wheeze
Clarify the complete controller regimen
why: A maintenance LABA is not interchangeable with the individualized reliever plan.
Device appearance does not establish the intended complete therapy.
Current comfort does not resolve a potentially unsafe maintenance regimen.
LABA monotherapy for asthma requires review because an appropriate anti-inflammatory component is needed.
takeaway: LABA monotherapy for asthma requires review because an appropriate anti-inflammatory component is needed.
learningObjective: Recognize that an asthma LABA regimen needs an appropriate inhaled anti-inflammatory plan.

title: Prevent nebulized anticholinergic eye exposure
stem: A client receiving nebulized ipratropium reports mist blowing into the eyes from a loose mask. What is the most useful correction?
options: Adjust the interface to prevent eye exposure
Ask the client to keep the eyes closed throughout every treatment
Increase nebulizer flow to finish sooner
Apply lubricating drops while maintaining the same mask fit
why: Proper fit limits local anticholinergic exposure that can cause eye problems.
Eye closure alone does not correct the leaking interface.
Faster delivery does not resolve misdirected medication.
Lubrication does not eliminate the medication exposure.
takeaway: Proper fit limits local anticholinergic exposure that can cause eye problems.
learningObjective: Correct mask leakage that directs nebulized ipratropium toward the eyes.

title: Assess possible theophylline toxicity
stem: A client taking theophylline develops repeated nausea, tremor and a rapid irregular pulse after a medication change. What is most appropriate?
options: Check the inhaler technique as the main response
Promptly review the medicines and assess possible toxicity
Give the next dose with food and reassess the nausea
Treat tremor as anxiety and review at the next clinic visit
why: Technique does not explain possible systemic theophylline toxicity.
Theophylline has a narrow therapeutic margin and this cluster suggests excessive exposure.
Food does not address the associated rhythm and neurological changes.
The combined symptoms merit a drug-toxicity assessment now.
takeaway: Theophylline has a narrow therapeutic margin and this cluster suggests excessive exposure.
learningObjective: Recognize nausea with cardiac and neurological stimulation during theophylline exposure.

title: Interpret increasing reliever use
stem: A client is comfortable today but reports using the prescribed reliever much more often over the last week. What is the best next step?
options: Judge control from today's clear breath sounds alone
Advise returning to the old use frequency regardless of symptoms
Review symptom control, technique and the asthma action plan
Request a larger refill as the complete response
why: A single examination misses the preceding symptom pattern.
Limiting use by instruction alone does not treat the underlying loss of control.
Increasing rescue use can signal deteriorating control even between acute episodes.
More supply does not investigate the reason for increased use.
takeaway: Increasing rescue use can signal deteriorating control even between acute episodes.
learningObjective: Use an increasing reliever pattern as a cue to reassess asthma control and technique.

title: Protect dry-powder inhaler delivery
stem: During return demonstration with a dry-powder inhaler, which actions support delivery when consistent with that device's instructions? Select all that apply.
options: Rinse the powder chamber immediately before each dose
Apply metered-dose inhaler timing instructions unchanged
Exhale away from the loaded device before inhaling
Use the instructed sufficiently forceful inhalation
Use a spacer attached to the powder mouthpiece
why: Water can compromise powder function; cleaning is device specific.
Different device mechanisms require different techniques.
Exhaled moisture can affect the powder if blown into the device.
Dry-powder delivery depends on the user's inspiratory effort for that device.
Spacers are generally designed for suitable metered-dose devices, not dry-powder inhalers.
takeaway: Exhaled moisture can affect the powder if blown into the device.
learningObjective: Recognize technique errors that introduce moisture or impair a dry-powder inhalation.

title: Report neuropsychiatric changes during montelukast
stem: A parent asks what changes to report after a child starts montelukast. Which new findings warrant prompt contact with the prescriber? Select all that apply.
options: New agitation, mood change or self-harm statements
Improved ability to join usual activities
A stable appetite matching the child's baseline
Less cough during the prescribed treatment period
Distressing nightmares and marked sleep disruption
why: These are important safety symptoms requiring timely assessment.
Functional improvement can reflect better symptom control.
An unchanged baseline pattern is not itself a new adverse-effect signal.
Reduced respiratory symptoms may represent the intended benefit.
Neuropsychiatric effects can include significant sleep changes.
takeaway: Neuropsychiatric effects can include significant sleep changes.
learningObjective: Include behavioural and mood warnings in teaching about montelukast.

title: Review an oral decongestant in hypertension
stem: A client with poorly controlled hypertension asks for oral pseudoephedrine for nasal congestion. What is appropriate?
options: Base the choice on the absence of nasal bleeding
Check suitability with the pharmacist or treatment team
Recommend the maximum package dose for faster relief
Choose a longer-acting preparation to reduce cardiovascular effects
why: Nasal bleeding is not the relevant measure of systemic drug safety.
Systemic sympathomimetic effects can raise pressure or cause palpitations.
A standard package maximum does not establish suitability for this client.
Longer duration does not remove the sympathomimetic risk.
takeaway: Systemic sympathomimetic effects can raise pressure or cause palpitations.
learningObjective: Assess sympathomimetic decongestant suitability in a client with uncontrolled blood pressure.

title: Recognize a first-generation antihistamine burden
stem: An older adult starts a sedating antihistamine and develops new functional problems. Which findings may be related? Select all that apply.
options: Improved itching with unchanged balance
A longstanding stable hearing deficit
Normal alertness with the usual bowel pattern
Increased sleepiness and unsteadiness
Dry mouth, constipation and difficulty voiding
why: Symptom improvement alone is not an adverse functional change.
An unchanged prior deficit does not indicate a new drug effect.
These findings do not support the reported sedative-anticholinergic burden.
Central sedation can increase impairment and falls risk.
This pattern is consistent with anticholinergic effects.
takeaway: Central sedation can increase impairment and falls risk.
learningObjective: Identify anticholinergic and sedative effects relevant to an older adult's medication review.

title: Evaluate prescribed lactulose treatment
stem: A client receives lactulose for hepatic encephalopathy. Which findings help evaluate the prescribed plan? Select all that apply.
options: Mental status improves toward baseline
Stool frequency meets the ordered target with stable hydration
Profuse diarrhea with postural dizziness
No change in cognition despite an increasing dose
Less appetite as the sole reported change
why: Improvement in encephalopathy is a clinically meaningful treatment outcome.
The bowel goal must be achieved without harmful fluid depletion.
Excessive losses suggest an adverse effect needing regimen review.
The lack of response requires reassessment rather than assuming efficacy.
Appetite alone does not establish treatment of encephalopathy.
takeaway: Improvement in encephalopathy is a clinically meaningful treatment outcome.
learningObjective: Balance encephalopathy improvement with bowel and hydration effects of lactulose.

title: Review bulk-forming fibre with swallowing limitations
stem: A client with significant dysphagia is prescribed a bulk-forming fibre product requiring a full fluid volume. They cannot safely take that volume. What is appropriate?
options: Clarify a suitable formulation or alternate bowel plan
Mix it into a very small amount to reduce swallowing effort
Administer the dry granules followed by a small sip
Divide the same dry amount across several spoonfuls
why: Adequate safe fluid intake is important to avoid choking or obstruction with bulk-forming agents.
Concentrating the preparation may create a swallowing or obstruction hazard.
Dry administration does not meet safe preparation requirements.
Dividing it does not resolve the required fluid and swallowing issue.
takeaway: Adequate safe fluid intake is important to avoid choking or obstruction with bulk-forming agents.
learningObjective: Assess whether a bulk-forming preparation is suitable when safe fluid intake is restricted.

title: Match pancreatic enzymes to food intake
stem: A client with pancreatic insufficiency is learning to use prescribed enzymes. Which instructions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
options: Report continuing greasy stools or weight loss
Take the entire daily amount on waking before food
Chew enteric-coated enzyme beads for faster action
Skip enzymes when the meal contains protein but little fat
Coordinate doses with meals and snacks as prescribed
why: Persistent malabsorption can indicate a need to review the regimen.
A single fasting dose does not accompany later meals.
Chewing can damage the protective coating and irritate oral tissue.
The individualized enzyme prescription may support digestion of more than fat alone.
Enzymes need to accompany food to support digestion.
takeaway: Enzymes need to accompany food to support digestion.
learningObjective: Teach meal-associated pancreatic enzyme use for prescribed malabsorption treatment.

title: Administer liquid iron while limiting staining
stem: A school-age child can swallow safely but has tooth staining from prescribed liquid iron. What teaching is appropriate?
options: Reduce the dose until the staining stops
Measure with a household spoon to avoid syringe contact
Use the instructed oral device toward the back of the mouth and rinse afterward
Mix the whole daily supply into a large jug of juice
why: A cosmetic effect does not authorize reducing prescribed treatment.
Household spoons reduce dose accuracy and do not solve tooth exposure.
Reducing tooth contact can limit staining while preserving accurate delivery.
The actual daily dose may become uncertain if the mixture is not fully consumed.
takeaway: Reducing tooth contact can limit staining while preserving accurate delivery.
learningObjective: Teach a practical technique that preserves the prescribed iron dose and reduces tooth exposure.

title: Explain replacement in pernicious anemia
stem: A client with pernicious anemia feels better and has an improved blood count after B12 treatment. They ask whether replacement is now unnecessary. What is best?
options: Use symptom disappearance alone to decide when treatment ends
Replace the prescribed plan with a standard multivitamin
Wait until anemia recurs before arranging further doses
Explain that the absorption problem may persist despite improvement
why: Neurological and hematological relapse may follow inadequate replacement.
Ordinary supplement dosing may not address the underlying absorption problem.
Reactive treatment permits preventable deficiency to return.
Correction of anemia does not restore intrinsic factor, so ongoing replacement is often required.
takeaway: Correction of anemia does not restore intrinsic factor, so ongoing replacement is often required.
learningObjective: Connect persistent intrinsic-factor deficiency with ongoing vitamin B12 replacement needs.

title: Distinguish folate correction from B12 evaluation
stem: A client with macrocytic anemia is being evaluated before replacement therapy. They also report foot numbness and gait change. What should the nurse highlight?
options: The neurological findings and the need to assess B12 status
Only the hemoglobin value when reporting replacement needs
Dietary folate intake as the sole assessment
Improvement in appetite as evidence that investigations can stop
why: Folate may improve blood counts while unrecognized B12-related neurological injury continues.
The neurological symptoms help distinguish causes and treatment risks.
Diet history does not exclude B12 deficiency or explain away neurological changes.
Appetite does not establish the cause of macrocytosis or nerve symptoms.
takeaway: Folate may improve blood counts while unrecognized B12-related neurological injury continues.
learningObjective: Recognize why neurological symptoms with macrocytosis require consideration of vitamin B12 deficiency.

title: Monitor blood pressure during epoetin therapy
stem: A client receiving epoetin for renal anemia has repeatedly elevated blood pressure and a new headache before a scheduled dose. What is appropriate?
options: Measure pressure again at the next monthly anemia review
Assess the symptoms and clarify dosing under the prescribed parameters
Use improving hemoglobin to approve the dose automatically
Move the injection to another site to reduce the pressure effect
why: Repeated elevation with headache warrants earlier assessment.
Epoetin treatment can worsen hypertension, making the new findings relevant before dosing.
Hematological benefit does not establish cardiovascular safety.
Changing the injection site does not correct systemic hypertension.
takeaway: Epoetin treatment can worsen hypertension, making the new findings relevant before dosing.
learningObjective: Recognize hypertension as a relevant safety concern during erythropoiesis-stimulating treatment.

title: Time phosphate binders with food
stem: A dialysis client takes all phosphate-binder tablets at bedtime because that is easiest to remember. What is the most useful teaching?
options: Use bedtime dosing whenever the daily total is unchanged
Take them after dialysis instead of with food
Link the prescribed doses to meals and relevant snacks
Take them when thirst is greatest
why: The same total can be less effective when separated from food.
Dialysis timing does not replace the food-binding requirement.
Binders act on dietary phosphate in the gastrointestinal tract.
Thirst does not determine when dietary phosphate is present.
takeaway: Binders act on dietary phosphate in the gastrointestinal tract.
learningObjective: Explain how a prescribed phosphate binder's action determines administration timing.

title: Assess calcium during calcitriol therapy
stem: A client taking calcitriol develops constipation, weakness and calcium above the supplied reference range. What should the nurse do?
options: Recommend an additional calcium supplement for weakness
Review only the phosphate value before the next dose
Advise taking calcitriol with more food to settle symptoms
Report the symptoms and calcium result for treatment review
why: More calcium may worsen the elevated level.
The symptomatic high calcium itself is a relevant safety finding.
Food timing does not address excessive calcium.
Active vitamin D therapy can contribute to hypercalcemia requiring reassessment.
takeaway: Active vitamin D therapy can contribute to hypercalcemia requiring reassessment.
learningObjective: Recognize symptoms and laboratory trends suggesting excessive calcium during active vitamin D therapy.

title: Evaluate prescribed bicarbonate in CKD
stem: A client with chronic kidney disease receives prescribed sodium bicarbonate for metabolic acidosis. Which follow-up is most relevant?
options: Bicarbonate trend, weight, edema and blood pressure
Urine colour and appetite as the complete evaluation
Only whether tablets are taken with meals
Only a normal potassium result after the first dose
why: Treatment response and sodium-related fluid tolerance both matter.
These do not measure acidosis correction or sodium burden adequately.
Adherence is relevant but does not establish physiological response.
Potassium alone cannot evaluate bicarbonate replacement and fluid effects.
takeaway: Treatment response and sodium-related fluid tolerance both matter.
learningObjective: Assess correction of metabolic acidosis alongside sodium-related fluid tolerance.

title: Review magnesium antacids in advanced kidney disease
stem: A client with advanced kidney disease uses a magnesium antacid several times daily. What should the nurse do?
options: Judge safety only by improvement in heartburn
Review the product and renal safety with the pharmacist or team
Approve continued use because it is available without prescription
Separate it from meals as the sole adjustment
why: Symptom relief can coexist with a systemic electrolyte adverse effect.
Reduced renal elimination can permit magnesium accumulation.
Nonprescription status does not establish safety in advanced renal disease.
Timing does not remove the renal accumulation concern.
takeaway: Reduced renal elimination can permit magnesium accumulation.
learningObjective: Identify potential accumulation from a nonprescription magnesium-containing product during renal impairment.

title: Reduce systemic absorption of eye drops
stem: A client prescribed timolol eye drops is taught nasolacrimal occlusion. Which actions fit the instructed technique? Select all that apply.
options: Rub the eye firmly after placing the drop
Add a second drop whenever some fluid reaches the cheek
Close the eyelid gently after instillation
Apply gentle pressure near the inner canthus for the taught interval
Blink rapidly to spread the medicine into the tear duct
why: Rubbing risks irritation and does not provide controlled occlusion.
Routine extra dosing can increase exposure beyond the prescription.
Gentle closure helps limit immediate drainage without forceful blinking.
Occluding drainage can reduce systemic absorption through the nasolacrimal pathway.
Rapid blinking promotes drainage rather than reducing it.
takeaway: Gentle closure helps limit immediate drainage without forceful blinking.
learningObjective: Teach prescribed nasolacrimal occlusion to reduce systemic exposure to ophthalmic timolol.

title: Space separately prescribed eye products
stem: A client must use two different eye-drop medicines at the same administration time. Which teaching points are appropriate? Select all that apply.
options: Verify the prescribed order when an ointment is also used
Mix both solutions in one dropper bottle
Place both drops rapidly to shorten the procedure
Use extra drops to compensate for any expected overflow
Follow the recommended interval between products
why: Ointments and drops may need a specific sequence for effective delivery.
Mixing can create contamination, stability and identification problems.
Immediate sequential instillation can increase washout.
Unplanned extra dosing does not provide reliable compensation.
Spacing reduces the chance that the next drop washes out the first.
takeaway: Spacing reduces the chance that the next drop washes out the first.
learningObjective: Prevent immediate washout when more than one ophthalmic product is prescribed.

title: Measure and handle nitroglycerin ointment safely
stem: A nurse applies prescribed nitroglycerin ointment. Which practice best supports accurate and safe handling?
options: Use the product's dose measure and appropriate gloves
Estimate an equivalent fingertip amount from memory
Rub it into bare skin with an ungloved hand
Use yesterday's application paper to maintain the same amount
why: A calibrated application method and skin protection limit dosing error and unintended exposure.
Visual estimation is less reliable than the intended product measure.
The nurse may absorb medication through direct skin contact.
Reusing material can leave an uncertain dose and contamination risk.
takeaway: A calibrated application method and skin protection limit dosing error and unintended exposure.
learningObjective: Use the prescribed measuring method while preventing unintended skin exposure during topical nitrate application.

title: Check a medicated patch before MRI
stem: A client wearing a medicated patch is scheduled for MRI. The product's backing composition is unknown. What is appropriate?
options: Cover it with another dressing before scanning
Verify MRI compatibility and the replacement plan
Leave it in place because its medicine is not magnetic
Remove it and discard the medication schedule
why: A covering does not establish protection against MRI-related heating.
Some patches contain material that can heat, while removal also affects medication delivery.
The backing material, not only the drug, can affect MRI safety.
If removal is needed, replacement timing must preserve safe therapy.
takeaway: Some patches contain material that can heat, while removal also affects medication delivery.
learningObjective: Use product and imaging guidance to manage a patch that may contain metal before MRI.

title: Evaluate epinephrine autoinjector readiness
stem: A client prescribed an epinephrine autoinjector practises with a trainer. Which findings support readiness? Select all that apply.
options: The client demonstrates the correct injection end and site
The client describes emergency help after use
The client practises by discharging part of the real rescue device
The client identifies readiness solely by memorizing the brand name
The client plans to judge expiry only from the box's appearance
why: Device-specific demonstration reduces delay and accidental injection risk.
Symptoms can persist or recur despite an initial response.
A partly used single-use product may not deliver its intended emergency dose.
Naming the product does not demonstrate administration skill.
Packaging appearance does not establish the stated expiry or product condition.
takeaway: Device-specific demonstration reduces delay and accidental injection risk.
learningObjective: Assess device-specific demonstration and the escalation plan after emergency epinephrine use.
